newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sanlam says to stop investing in S.African CBDs.
newsitem.headline: Sanlam says to stop investing in S.African CBDs.

text.p: South Africa's largest property investor Sanlam Properties said on Tuesday that it would no longer invest in the country's central business districts (CBDs) due to the flight of commerce in the face of a crime wave.
South Africa is plagued by violent crime against people and property that has seen some city centres, such as that of Johannesburg, become virtual no-go areas after dark.
Sanlam Properties managing director Banus van der Walt said the areas now had huge amounts of vacant space as business fled to out-of-town locations.
"Vacant space in commercial buildings represents idle capital and has a negative impact on investments and the profit of companies," he said.
He said Sanlam will cease to invest CBDs until the problem is solved.
He blamed crime as the main reason. "First and foremost is the increase in crime. People do not feel safe going to work or shopping in the CBDs," he said.

Van der Walt said all South Africa's main cities shared the problem with about 300,000 square metres of vacant space in the Johannesburg CBD, 71,500 in Cape Town's, 88,000 in Durban's and 129,000 in Pretoria's.
He warned that the whole economy was suffering. "The country cannot afford so much unused space and it does not contribute to real economic growth," he said.
He also warned that the problem was spreading out from the CBDs and hitting the new business centres, such as Johannesburg's Rosebank area.
"There is also a trend that crime is expanding to decentralised areas which can lead to these areas becoming as undesirable as the CBDs," he said.
Sanlam also believes the problem is exacerbated by poor infrastructure, such as parking, and the fact that too many purpose-built business parks are springing up outside the traditional CBDs.
Van der Walt said the government must act to tackle crime and tempt businesses back to city centres by suitable legislation.
"Sanlam Properties appeals to the government to take steps to ensure that the country's economy does not buckle under the crime wave," he said.
Many of South Africa's largest property firms have huge assets locked up in the country's CBDs and the industry fears it cannot afford to let the situation deteriorate any further.
